title: Is juice jacking real
caption:
Is juice jacking real? The FBI warned about public USB chargers, but its post named no case.
Researchers did pull it off in a lab, and your phone asks before it shares data.
Ever tapped Trust on a public port? Yes or no?
keywords: is it safe to charge phone at airport
pinned_comment: Honest version: lab attacks exist (in 2025, TU Graz researchers built a charger that got past the prompt on phones from 8 vendors), and the FBI post named no case. So a public charger probably isn't hacking you, but at a public port, never tap Trust or Allow. Ever tapped Trust on a public port? Yes or no?

pinned_backups.reply: No. Researchers at TU Graz made it work in a lab in 2025, with "a custom cheap malicious charger design". What the FBI post didn't do is name a real case. So: probably not happening to you, but never tap Trust or Allow on a public port.

pinned_backups.reply: Apple's own reset: Settings › General › Transfer or Reset iPhone › Reset › Reset Location & Privacy. Apple says it resets "the computers you've chosen to trust". Next time tap Don't Trust; charging still works.
No. Don't Trust blocks the data, not the power. Google's Pixel page says the same for its USB Protection: "Charging through USB continues to function even with a locked screen."
None of the sources we used test them, so the video doesn't recommend one. The FBI's own advice: "Carry your own charger and USB cord and use an electrical outlet instead."

pinned_backups.reply: Google says "Some of these steps only work on Android 14 and up", and menus vary by maker. Leave it on charging only at a public port; don't pick File Transfer.

youtube_description:
Is it safe to charge your phone at the airport? Juice jacking, a public USB charger that steals your data or plants malware, has been pulled off by researchers in a lab. But the FBI post that warned travelers about it named no case. Your phone also asks before a USB port gets your data: an iPhone shows "Trust This Computer?", and Android waits until you choose File Transfer. So a public charger probably isn't hacking you, but at a public port never tap Trust or Allow. Or skip the port and use your own wall plug.

FBI Denver on X, April 6, 2023: "Avoid using free charging stations in airports, hotels or shopping centers. Bad actors have figured out ways to use public USB ports to introduce malware and monitoring software onto devices. Carry your own charger and USB cord and use an electrical outlet instead." The post names no case, place, date or victim. It is one post from the FBI's Denver field office. The video says "plant"; the FBI's word is "introduce".

Apple, "About the 'Trust This Computer' alert message on your iPhone, iPad, or iPod touch": "When you connect your iPhone, iPad, or iPod touch to a computer or other device for the first time, an alert message asks whether you trust the computer…" "Trusted computers can sync with your device and access your device's photos, videos, contacts, and other content." "If you don't want to trust the computer or other connected device, tap Don't Trust on your device." To undo a Trust, Apple's reset: Settings › General › Transfer or Reset iPhone › Reset › Reset Location & Privacy.

Google, Android Help, "Transfer files between your computer & Android device": "On your device, tap the "Charging this device via USB" notification. Under "Use USB for," select File Transfer." And: "Important: Some of these steps only work on Android 14 and up." Scope: Android 14 and up; menus vary by phone maker.

Google, Android Help, "Protect your Android device from USB threats with Advanced Protection Mode": "When you connect a USB device, you may receive notifications that’ll prompt you to unlock your screen and allow data transfer through USB." "Charging through USB continues to function even with a locked screen." "This feature is available on Pixel 6 and later devices." Scope: Pixel 6 and later, with Advanced Protection's USB Protection on; Google also lists "No protection when the device is unlocked".

Draschbacher, Maar, Oberhuber and Mangard (Graz University of Technology), "ChoiceJacking: Compromising Mobile Devices through Malicious Chargers like a Decade ago", USENIX Security 2025: "…mobile OSs introduced user prompts for confirming data connections from a USB host to a mobile device." Their lab attack, built on "a custom cheap malicious charger design", is "…the first to bypass existing JuiceJacking mitigations" and gained access to user files "…on all tested devices from 8 vendors including the top 6 by market share." "All but one (including Google, Samsung, Xiaomi, and Apple) acknowledged our attacks and are in the process of integrating mitigations."

Fine print: The FBI post names no confirmed real-world case, but that doesn't mean juice jacking is impossible; the 2025 lab result shows a charger can fake the tap, and phone makers are still adding fixes. This video doesn't say any phone or OS version is fully protected. The iPhone alert, the Android screen and the FBI post are drawn and re-created by hand; no real interface, post or logo is shown. Not affiliated with Apple, Google, the FBI, TU Graz, USENIX or anyone else.
